subject: research/selfrep-platepack
professional: an operations-research / manufacturing-systems researcher (lot sizing and setup-time batching in job shops) who also knows FDM printing practice; first checks the DES against an independent implementation, then whether the plate sizes are physically printable and whether the setup-versus-batch trade-off is already textbook

evidence.correctness: Ran `python3 experiments/run.py` (11 s): results.txt regenerated byte-identical (git status clean), so every table cell reproduces. Independent recomputation with my own scratch simulator (not importing partpool) in the noiseless case, 24 cells (k in {1,4,11,44} x changeover {0,0.25,1} x whole/focus), matched simulate(cv=0) exactly in all 24: whole = 6 generations x (44/k*(k+c)+6), e.g. k=11,c=0.25 -> 306.0 h; focus k=1,c=0 -> 259.0 h (equals the partpool README's 259 h), k=44 focus = whole (300/301.5/306 h). Also recomputed README headline numbers from results.txt table C (best k 1/4/11/11; gains 15.5/12.1/10.2/7.6 % = 1 - focus/whole) and they agree. Not independently recomputed: the stochastic medians (only reproduced, not re-derived by a second implementation). One modelling confound found: the lognormal CV 0.2 applies per job, so a 44-part plate has 44x the relative variance of the sum of 44 one-part jobs; rescaling cv to 0.2/sqrt(k) moves k=44 from 52.5 h to 50.8 h (about 3%) while k=1 is unchanged, so part of the 'big plates are worse' effect is a noise artefact the README does not disclose.
evidence.completeness: Every README feature checked: 8 tests exist and pass (`python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v`, 8 OK); run.py produces results.txt with sections A, B, C; figure.py regenerated plate_size.svg identically; README bullets for all four changeovers, the pooling gain and the k=44 equals whole claim all match results.txt; research/README.md bullet and _homepage/projects.json entry present. Failure modelling and real masses are declared as next steps, not claimed. No stubs or dead code found.
evidence.verification: Test command: unittest discover, 8 tests, all pass in 0.01 s. They check invariants (plate count, work independent of k, changeover adds per plate, single printer deterministic time, ordering) but none checks a stochastic result, results.txt against run.py, or asm_h/cv pass-through. Seeded mutation 1: changeover dropped for k=44 (`changeover_h if k < 44 else 0.0` in plated), which changes whole's headline best-k rows: all 8 tests still passed (SURVIVED). Seeded mutation 2: asm_h parameter ignored (ASSEMBLY_H hard-coded): all 8 passed (SURVIVED). Both reverted with git checkout. test_figure only parses the committed text. 0 of 2 mutations caught, so tests would miss real bugs in the plate model beyond the covered invariants.
evidence.craft: Read model.py, run.py, figure.py, both test files, and partpool/model.py which it imports. Positives: reuses partpool by import, not copy; plated() validates k; figure parsed from results.txt via shared linefig. Defects: `import math` unused in the test; sys.path.insert hacks with parents[3] depend on sibling directories while pyproject declares dependencies=[] and a setuptools package, so the package cannot be installed or run alone; no confidence intervals or paired-difference statistics although common random numbers are used, and differences such as k=1 vs 2 at c=0 (43.2 vs 43.6) are claimed as an ordering with no uncertainty; results.txt hard-codes the changeover list in two files; run.py is a flat script with no main guard; in the inherited simulator `if policy == 'whole': free.append(w) else: free.append(w)` is a duplicated branch.
evidence.claims: Checked each README number against experiments/results.txt: best k 1 (43.2), 4 (46.4), 11 (47.8), 11 (49.6); k=1 at 1 h = 78.3; k=44 focus 52.5 equals whole; pooling gains 15.5/12.1/10.2/7.6 %; whole best k=44 from c=0.25; '8 tests'; 'about 10 s' (11 s measured). All backed. The README labels the work stylised, says masses are placeholders, bed area and plate failure are unmodelled and that the result is the trend not the k. Gaps: the per-job CV noise confound above is not disclosed; no interval on the orderings; 'Produced with AI assistance' present. No fabricated inputs; changeover values are honestly marked assumed.
evidence.fitness: A researcher could extend it (clean model, README names failure probability and real masses as next steps) but would hit three walls quickly: parts are identical so packing is trivially k x one part; k=22 and k=44 plates are not physically printable on a Prusa-class bed, so half the swept grid is outside the real feasible set; and the headline (optimal batch size grows with setup time, pooling gives a bounded gain) is the textbook lot-sizing result. Nearest prior work, none cited: Karmarkar, 'A study of lotsizing and queueing', Management Science 1985 / Hopp and Spearman, Factory Physics (batching with setup, U-shaped cycle time against batch size); Economic lot size (Harris 1913); Moses and Chirikjian, 'Robotic self-replication', Annual Review of Control, Robotics, and Autonomous Systems 2020; Freitas and Merkle, Kinematic Self-Replicating Machines 2004; Jones et al., Robotica 2011 (RepRap, cited). The novel part is only the specific coupling to the focus/whole replication policies; the result is not new in kind and is not yet publishable. It does cite and build on partpool, growth and closure.
evidence.domain: A manufacturing-systems reviewer would object that: setup-time batching has a closed-form and queueing literature (sqrt-type optimum) that the simulation neither uses nor checks against; uniform 1 h parts remove the actual packing problem (bed area, part height, support, multi-colour/material changes) so the studied k are not real plates; a plate failure loses all its parts and is excluded (README admits it favours big plates, which is the direction of the headline); changeover is modelled as a fixed per-plate time though heat-up overlaps the previous job on real printers and bed clearing can be done by another worker; assembly by a printer is unrealistic (inherited). The method is a sound toy DES, honestly labelled, but a practitioner would not sign off the plate sizes.

defects.what: Seeded mutations in plated() (changeover dropped for k=44, asm_h ignored) both pass all 8 tests; no test pins a stochastic output or the pass-through of asm_h and cv.

Per-job CV 0.2 is applied to the plate job, so big plates carry far more relative variance than the sum of the same parts; rescaling to 0.2/sqrt(k) changes k=44 from 52.5 h to 50.8 h. The README attributes the big-plate penalty to lost pooling only and does not disclose this confound.
k=22 and k=44 plates (and arguably 11) are not physically printable on a typical bed, and parts are identical, so the swept range is partly infeasible; headline k=11 depends on that.
Orderings (for example k=1 vs 2 at c=0, 43.2 vs 43.6 h) reported with no interval though common random numbers make a paired CI cheap.

pyproject declares no dependencies and an installable package but the code imports sibling selfrep-partpool and selfrep-closure by relative path; unused import math in test_platepack.py; no cited lot-sizing prior work.

verdict: A small, honest, reproducible stylised study: all 29 lines of results.txt regenerate byte for byte, the noiseless cases match an independent implementation in 24 of 24 cells, and every README number matches the results file with its limits stated, so correctness, claims and completeness are at the bar. It does not meet the bar overall: the tests missed both seeded mutations (verification 2), the result is the textbook setup-versus-batch trade-off with no cited lot-sizing literature and parts that cannot physically share plates of 22 or 44 (fitness 2, domain 2), and an undisclosed per-job noise confound inflates the big-plate penalty by about 3%. Median 2 of 7. A researcher could extend it with failure probability and real masses, but it is a toy extension of partpool rather than a result to cite.
